lesson.title: Bookends for a Message: The 5' Cap and Poly-A Tail
lesson.summary: Eukaryotic pre-mRNA is modified at both ends, a modified guanine cap at the 5' end and a long stretch of adenine nucleotides at the 3' end, and these two additions protect the transcript and mark it as ready for export and translation.
lesson.body:
As soon as RNA polymerase II starts transcribing a gene, and before the transcript is even finished, the cell already begins protecting it. Recall from mRNA processing that a raw pre-mRNA is not yet a working messenger; it still needs modification before it can leave the nucleus and be read by a ribosome. The first change happens almost immediately at the 5' end: an enzyme attaches a modified guanine nucleotide, methylated at a specific position, to the very start of the growing chain. What makes this cap unusual is the bond that attaches it. Every other linkage in an RNA strand runs 5' to 3', but the cap is joined through a reversed 5' to 5' bond. That backward orientation is exactly why it works so well as protection: enzymes in the cell that chew through RNA starting at a normal 5' end have nothing to grab onto, so the capped transcript resists degradation far longer than an uncapped one would.

The 3' end gets a matching kind of protection, added by a different mechanism. Once RNA polymerase transcribes past a specific signal sequence in the pre-mRNA, most commonly AAUAAA, the transcript is cut at that site, and an enzyme called poly-A polymerase adds a long run of adenine nucleotides, the poly-A tail, without copying them from any DNA template. In mammalian mRNAs this tail typically runs from around one hundred to a few hundred adenines. Just as the cap blocks attack from the 5' end, the poly-A tail keeps exonucleases from chewing in from the 3' end, buying the message more time to be used before it is destroyed.

Protection from degradation is only part of why these two modifications matter. Both are also required for the mature mRNA to be exported out of the nucleus through the nuclear pores, and both are recognized directly by the translation machinery once the message reaches the cytoplasm. The cap is bound by an initiation factor that helps position the ribosome at the start of the message, while the poly-A tail is bound by poly-A-binding proteins that can reach back and interact with proteins sitting on the cap. That interaction effectively bends the mRNA into a loop, bringing its two ends close together. The loop shape helps ribosomes that finish translating recycle quickly back to the start, which makes each capped and tailed message more efficient to translate repeatedly. In short, the cap and tail are not decorations on the message; they are what make a fragile, freshly transcribed pre-mRNA into a stable, exportable, translatable piece of information.
